title: How Labor Unions Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how labor unions work, prompted by listener requests and the 2011 Wisconsin fight over Governor Scott Walker's bill stripping public-sector collective bargaining. They trace unions from medieval trade guilds through the nineteenth-century Industrial Revolution, violent strikes, the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, and the Haymarket affair that led to May Day and the Labor Day holiday. They cover bargaining units, collective bargaining agreements, dues, local unions, union wage and benefit statistics, criticisms of unions, the National Labor Relations Act and NLRB, Taft-Hartley, the Landrum-Griffin style Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act, union membership decline and income inequality, and the Teamsters and Jimmy Hoffa. The episode ends with a listener mail about DonorsChoose.org and sign-off.
topics: Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act

segments.title: Opening banter and the Wisconsin union fight
segments.summary: Hosts joke about podcasting and introduce the topic of labor unions, citing last year's Wisconsin protests over Governor Scott Walker's bill that stripped public-sector collective bargaining and required pension contributions. They note Pew poll findings that Americans view organized labor positively while many see unions as a necessary evil.

segments.title: Origins: trade guilds and the Industrial Revolution
segments.summary: Trade guilds in medieval Europe are described as the seeds of unions, originally for sharing techniques and later for expertise and wages. In the nineteenth century, factory conditions were poor, and the Triangle Shirtwaist fire became a turning point for bringing working conditions into view.

segments.title: Violent nineteenth-century strikes and the Haymarket affair
segments.summary: Strikes in the nineteenth century were far more violent, with National Guard, police and Pinkerton detectives confronting workers. The Haymarket riot in Chicago, a bomb and gunfire during a nationwide eight-hour-day strike, led to convictions, executions and a suicide, and the later pardon of remaining prisoners. Grover Cleveland then moved the federal Labor Day to September.

segments.title: Basics: bargaining units, collective bargaining agreements, and dues
segments.summary: A union forms a bargaining unit with an elected leader to negotiate with the employer. The resulting collective bargaining agreement (CBA) sets terms for a fixed period and is enforced through grievances and arbitration. Unions are funded by member dues, often described as around fifty dollars a month, and locals operate as chapters of national charters. Democratic elections of leaders are the ideal.

segments.title: Union benefits, statistics and protection from unjust firing
segments.summary: Statistics cited from the Department of Labor show union members earn higher median weekly income than non-union workers and are more likely to have health, dental and vision coverage. Women, African Americans and Latinos earn more in unions. Unions protect workers from unjust dismissal, illustrated by a Florida law firm case involving workers who wore orange shirts.

segments.title: Criticisms of unions and political divide
segments.summary: Criticisms include unions shielding poor performers, harming competitiveness, and state employee pensions draining budgets. The hosts note that opinions often follow political lines, though Republicans backed unions historically; Eisenhower praised union rights, and unions supported Medicare, Social Security and civil rights, with a quote from Congressman Richard Bolling on the Civil Rights Act.

segments.title: Union decline and rising income inequality
segments.summary: Union membership peaked around 35 percent of non-agricultural workers in the 1950s and is now about 11.8 percent, with under 7 percent in the private sector. Bruce Western and Jake Rosenfeld's paper links the decline of unions since the 1970s to about a third of the rise in US income inequality. The hosts tie this to business mobilizing in Washington.

segments.title: Federal labor law: NLRA, NLRB, Taft-Hartley and Landrum-Griffin
segments.summary: The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 required employers to negotiate in good faith and created the NLRB, protecting union elections and anti-discrimination. Exclusions included agricultural, domestic, government and rail/airline workers. Taft-Hartley allowed injunctions for strikes endangering public health and outlawed secondary boycotts. Hosts discuss Reagan firing air traffic controllers. The Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act added election safeguards and reporting to curb mob influence.

segments.title: Strike funds, AFL-CIO, Teamsters and Jimmy Hoffa
segments.summary: Unions often keep strike funds that pay members during strikes. The AFL-CIO is described as a federation of dozens of member unions, formed when the AFL merged with the CIO. The Teamsters are noted for their size and Jimmy Hoffa's disappearance amid mob ties, with his son James P. Hoffa now leading the union.

segments.title: Digression on comedy and humor
segments.summary: The hosts digress into a discussion about comedian Gilbert Godfrey's firing over Twitter jokes about the Japanese tsunami and the importance of a sense of humor and edgy comedy.

segments.title: Personal union connections and closing recap
segments.summary: Chuck mentions his parents were in the teachers union, and the hosts recap that opinions on unions often depend on family background. They suggest the article on how unions work and a Washington Post editorial on the Wisconsin fight as further reading.

segments.title: Listener mail: DonorsChoose.org
segments.summary: A listener from DonorsChoose.org promotes the nonprofit that lets people fund public school classroom requests. Hosts also discuss a listener who says a system admin sounds like Josh, and ask for listener stories about strikes and police encounters.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and close the episode with a brief sponsor line.
